What is CI/CD? CI vs Continuous Delivery vs Continuous Deployment?

CI: every commit is built and tested automatically, so problems are found early. Continuous Delivery: every build is releasable, and production deploys need a manual approval. Continuous Deployment: every passing build goes to production automatically.
What is Jenkins? Controller–agent architecture?

An open-source automation server with more than 1800 plugins. The controller (formerly "master") hosts the UI, configuration and scheduling. Agents (nodes) run the builds and connect over SSH or JNLP, or run as Docker or Kubernetes pods. Executors are the build slots on each agent.
Declarative vs Scripted pipeline?

Declarative (pipeline { }): a structured, opinionated syntax with built-in post, when, options and validation. This is the recommended style. Scripted (node { }): full Groovy, more flexible but harder to maintain. Declarative can embed script { } blocks.
What is a Jenkinsfile and why keep it in Git?
Pipeline-as-code. It's versioned and reviewed alongside the app, gives each branch its own pipeline (Multibranch Pipeline), and is reproducible and auditable.
How are builds triggered?
SCM webhooks (GitHub or Bitbucket push, PR) · pollSCM · cron (scheduled builds) · upstream or downstream jobs · manual runs or parameters · the remote API.
How do you manage secrets/credentials?

Use the Credentials plugin (username/password, secret text, SSH key, certificate), accessed through credentials() or withCredentials. Jenkins masks them in logs. Never hard-code secrets. You can integrate with Vault.
What is a Multibranch Pipeline / Shared Library?

Multibranch: Jenkins scans the repo and creates a pipeline automatically for every branch or PR that has a Jenkinsfile. Shared Library: reusable Groovy steps (vars/, src/) kept in a separate repo and loaded with @Library('my-lib') _, so pipelines stay DRY across many services.
post conditions in a pipeline?
always, success, failure, unstable (for example, failing tests), changed, fixed, regression, aborted, cleanup. Used for notifications, publishing test reports, and workspace cleanup.

Common plugins you've used?
Git, Pipeline, Blue Ocean, Credentials Binding, Docker Pipeline, Kubernetes, SonarQube Scanner, JUnit, JaCoCo, Slack Notification, Role-based Authorization, Artifactory or Nexus, Email Extension.
Jenkins vs GitHub Actions vs GitLab CI?

Jenkins is self-hosted, highly customizable through plugins, and heavier to maintain. GitHub Actions and GitLab CI are SaaS-native, configured in YAML, and tightly integrated with their repositories. They're increasingly common in newer projects.
Why is it recommended to have 0 executors on the controller?

Security first: a build on the controller runs as the Jenkins user with access to JENKINS_HOME, including encrypted credentials and their keys, so a malicious or buggy build can read all of them. Second, stability: builds compete for CPU and memory with the UI and the scheduler, and a runaway build can bring down the service. Use separate agents, ideally ephemeral containers.
What runs on the agent and what runs on the controller in a Pipeline?

Steps such as sh, bat and checkout run on the agent. The Groovy logic that surrounds them runs on the controller, in the CPS engine. So new File('x').text in a Jenkinsfile reads the file on the controller, not the workspace. Use readFile, fileExists and writeFile, which are steps and do run on the agent. It also explains why heavy Groovy loops slow Jenkins for everyone.
Why does a Pipeline survive a controller restart? What does that require?

The engine saves the program's position after each step, and steps such as sh run as separate durable processes on the agent, tracked through log files. After a restart, the build resumes where it stopped. This requires serializable local variables, which is why NotSerializableException occurs. Durability settings (MAX_SURVIVABILITY, SURVIVABLE_NONATOMIC, PERFORMANCE_OPTIMIZED) trade this safety against disk writes. Freestyle jobs do not resume.
SUCCESS vs UNSTABLE vs FAILURE vs ABORTED?

SUCCESS: all fine. UNSTABLE: the build ran, but a quality step reported problems, typically junit found test failures. FAILURE: a step failed, such as a non-zero sh exit. ABORTED: stopped by a user, a timeout or a newer build. By default, later stages still run after UNSTABLE, so gate deployment with when { expression { currentBuild.currentResult == 'SUCCESS' } }, or use junit and fail the build deliberately. To record a stage failure and continue, use catchError(buildResult: 'SUCCESS', stageResult: 'FAILURE') { ... }.
What's the difference between environment, withEnv, withCredentials and params?

environment defines variables for the pipeline or a stage, set before steps run. withEnv(['A=1']) { } does the same for a block, and is useful in scripted code. withCredentials binds secrets for a block, and they are masked in logs. params.X reads a build parameter. Note that params values are typed (a boolean parameter is a real boolean), while environment variables are always strings, so env.FLAG == 'true' is needed.
What does sh 'echo $BUILD_NUMBER ${env.BUILD_NUMBER}' do?

Single-quoted Groovy strings are not interpolated, so the text goes to the shell unchanged. The shell expands $BUILD_NUMBER correctly, but ${env.BUILD_NUMBER} is not valid shell, so it fails with a "bad substitution" error. In double quotes, Groovy expands both before the shell sees them. Rule: use single quotes with shell variables, double quotes for Groovy variables, and escape with \$ to pass one through to the shell.
How do you avoid rebuilding the same image for each environment?

Build once in CI, tag the image with the Git SHA or build number, and push. Later stages only re-deploy that tag with a different configuration (Helm values, Kubernetes ConfigMaps and Secrets, environment variables). Spring profiles or external config handle backend differences. For Angular, load a config.json at start-up, since build-time environment.ts values would force a rebuild per environment. Promote by digest for a tamper-proof reference.
How do you speed up a slow pipeline?

- Find the slow stage using stage view timings.
- Cache dependencies: a shared .m2, a registry cache, npm ci with a cache.
- Run tests in parallel: parallel stages, Surefire forkCount, the Parallel Test Executor plugin.
- Do not repeat work: build once and stash.
- Run expensive checks only where needed, using changeset or path filters in a monorepo.
- Use layer caching in Docker, and put COPY pom.xml before the sources.
- Use a shallow clone in checkout.
How do you scale Jenkins?

The controller scales mostly by being kept light, and agents scale horizontally. Use the Kubernetes plugin for ephemeral pod agents that are created per build. For many teams, split into several controllers per organisation or department rather than one huge instance, since one controller is a single point of failure and open-source Jenkins has no built-in active-active mode. Keep build logs small, discard old builds, and store artifacts in Nexus or S3.
How do you back up and restore Jenkins?

Back up JENKINS_HOME, in particular config.xml, jobs/, users/, plugins/ and secrets/. Without secrets/, stored credentials cannot be decrypted, so store that directory securely. Workspaces and caches can be skipped. The modern method is to rebuild, not restore: Jenkins in a Docker image with pinned plugins, JCasC for configuration, Job DSL or Organization Folders for jobs. Then only build history and secrets need backing up.
stash vs archiveArtifacts?

stash keeps files for reuse later in the same build on another agent, and they are removed at the end of the build. archiveArtifacts stores files with the build record on the controller, downloadable afterwards. Neither is designed for huge files: for real release artifacts, publish to Nexus, Artifactory or S3.
How do you implement a rollback?

With immutable versioned images, a rollback is a redeployment of the last good tag. helm rollback shop reverts the release, and helm upgrade --atomic does so automatically on failure. A parameterised job can take a version as input. Database changes make this harder. Use backward-compatible migrations (expand, migrate, contract) with Flyway, so that old code still works against the new schema. A rollback is safest when a deployment is decoupled from a release through feature flags.
Blue-green vs canary vs rolling deployment?

Strategy | How it works | Trade-off
Rolling | Replace instances a few at a time. Kubernetes default | No extra cost, but two versions run together
Blue-green | Run a full new environment, then switch traffic at once | Instant rollback, double resources
Canary | Send a small share of traffic to the new version and increase it while watching metrics | Lowest risk, needs traffic control and good monitoring
How would you run integration tests that need MySQL and Kafka?

Use Testcontainers in the Maven verify phase, which starts real containers from test code. The agent needs access to a Docker daemon, which can be the host's socket, or a Docker-in-Docker sidecar in Kubernetes. Mounting the host socket gives the build root-equivalent access to the host, so only do this on dedicated, trusted agents. Alternatives are docker compose up in a stage with teardown in post { always { } }, or a sidecar container in a Kubernetes agent pod.
How does the SonarQube quality gate work in a Pipeline?

withSonarQubeEnv injects the server URL and token. The scanner uploads the analysis, and SonarQube processes it asynchronously in a background task. Then waitForQualityGate pauses the pipeline. It needs a webhook configured in SonarQube pointing to https://jenkins.example.com/sonarqube-webhook/. Without it, the step waits until the timeout. The gate typically checks new code for coverage, duplication, and no new critical issues. With abortPipeline: true, a failed gate fails the build.
What are Docker agents vs Kubernetes agents vs static agents?

Static agents are always-on machines. They are simple and allow caches, but drift over time and cost money when idle. Docker agents (agent { docker { } }) run the stage inside a container on a host, giving a pinned toolchain. Kubernetes agents are pods created per build, possibly with several containers (maven, node, docker) and a container('maven') { } block choosing where a step runs. They scale well and leave no state, but need external caching.
Scenario: two pipelines deploy at once and overwrite each other. Fix it.

Add disableConcurrentBuilds() within a job. Across jobs, use a lock(resource: 'env-name') from the Lockable Resources plugin. Add milestone steps so that an older build cannot deploy after a newer one has passed that point. On the target side, Helm refuses a concurrent release while another operation is in progress, and Kubernetes rollouts are idempotent, which adds a further safety net.
Scenario: a secret appears in the build log. What do you do?

- Treat it as compromised and rotate it first; deleting logs does not undo exposure.
- Delete the affected build logs, and check anyone who could see them.
- Find the cause: often set -x, a Groovy-interpolated string, or an encoded or transformed value that the mask cannot match.
- Fix the script, and use short-lived credentials where possible.
- Add secret scanning, such as Gitleaks, to the pipeline.
Scenario: design CI/CD for 30 microservices.

Give each service its own repository or a monorepo with path filters, and an Organization Folder to discover them. Keep a one-line Jenkinsfile that calls a versioned shared-library pipeline, so a change to the process is made in one place. Stages: build, unit test, contract tests (Pact or Spring Cloud Contract), SonarQube, image build, image scan (Trivy), push. For deployment, use a GitOps tool such as Argo CD, which watches a config repository that CI updates with the new tag. Progress from dev to staging to production with automated checks and canary analysis. Use Kubernetes agents, a central dashboard, and DORA metrics (deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate, time to restore).
What's a Dockerfile layout for fast, small Spring Boot and Angular images?

# Spring Boot: multi-stage, layered
FROM maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-21 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY pom.xml .
RUN mvn -B -q dependency:go-offline      # cached unless pom.xml changes
COPY src ./src
RUN mvn -B -q -DskipTests package
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre
RUN useradd -r app
USER app
COPY --from=build /src/target/*.jar /app.jar
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "/app.jar"]
# Angular: build with Node, serve with nginx
FROM node:22-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY package*.json .
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npx ng build --configuration production
FROM nginx:alpine
COPY --from=build /src/dist/ui/browser /usr/share/nginx/html
COPY nginx.conf /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf
Copying dependency files before the source keeps layer caching useful. The runtime stage holds no build tools. Run as non-root. The exact Angular output folder depends on the project name in angular.json.
How do you test a Jenkinsfile change safely?

Push to a branch, as Multibranch runs that branch's own Jenkinsfile. Use Replay to try an edit without a commit. Lint it through the declarative validator endpoint or a CLI. For shared libraries, write unit tests with JenkinsPipelineUnit and load a branch of the library with @Library('lib@feature-x'). Guard deployment stages with when { branch 'main' }, so that test branches cannot reach production.
What is pipeline-as-code's benefit over clicking in the UI?

The process lives next to the code it builds, so it is reviewed in PRs, versioned, and consistent with the code at any commit. A branch can change its own build. An old release can be rebuilt with its original pipeline. Disaster recovery is easier, because no knowledge lives only in a controller's XML files. Audit is simpler, since Git shows who changed what.
What is the difference between input as a stage directive and as a step?

The directive (stage { input { message '...' } steps { } }) is evaluated before the stage enters its agent, so a stage-level agent is not held while waiting. It also applies before when, unless you set beforeInput true in the when. The step (input message: '...' in steps) runs wherever it is, so inside an agent stage it occupies an executor for the whole wait. Either way, wrap it with a timeout, so an unanswered build does not stay open indefinitely. A top-level agent any also holds an executor, which is why long approvals call for agent none.
How do you handle a flaky test or a flaky network step?

For network calls, wrap the step in retry(3) { sh '...' }, or use options { retry(2) } on a stage. In Kubernetes agents, retry(count: 2, conditions: [kubernetesAgent(), nonresumable()]) re-runs only on agent loss. For tests, retrying only hides bugs, so report them: Surefire's rerunFailingTestsCount labels flaky tests, and then you can track and fix them. Never let a retry hide a real failure in a deployment stage, since a repeated deployment may not be idempotent.

How can a Jenkins job be triggered from a script?

Call the REST API with a user's API token: curl -X POST -u user:token "https://jenkins.example.com/job/deploy/buildWithParameters?TARGET=staging". API tokens do not need the CSRF crumb that session-based requests do. The response's Location header gives the queue item, which you can poll for the build number. Add /api/json to most Jenkins URLs for JSON data. The jenkins-cli.jar client is an alternative.
How do you trigger another job from a Pipeline and pass parameters?

Use the build step: build job: 'deploy-orders', parameters: [string(name: 'TAG', value: env.GIT_COMMIT)], wait: true, propagate: true. With wait: false it fires and forgets; propagate: false lets the caller continue even if the downstream job fails (you can inspect the returned build's result). The declarative triggers { upstream('build-orders') } does the reverse — start this job when another finishes. 💡 Prefer one pipeline with stages over long chains of jobs; chains are hard to trace.
In a monorepo, how do you build only what changed?

Use when { changeset 'backend/**' } on a stage so it runs only if files under that path changed, or compute changed paths with git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD. Build tools help too: Maven -pl module -am builds one module and its dependencies, and Nx/Turborepo do affected-only builds for Angular. Always run the full build on main or nightly as a safety net, because path filters can miss shared-library changes.
What is CPS in Jenkins Pipeline and when do you need @NonCPS?

Pipeline Groovy is transformed into Continuation-Passing Style so that the program state can be serialised to disk — that is how a build survives a controller restart. The side effect is that some Groovy/Java features behave oddly (closures in each, non-serialisable objects like Matcher held across steps cause NotSerializableException). @NonCPS marks a helper method to run as plain Groovy; it must be fast, must not call pipeline steps such as sh or echo, and its locals are not persisted. 💡 Best fix: keep logic in shell scripts or a shared library, and keep the Jenkinsfile thin.
Which security checks would you add to a CI pipeline?

Secret scanning (Gitleaks), dependency/SCA scanning (OWASP Dependency-Check, Snyk, npm audit), SAST (SonarQube security rules, CodeQL), container image scanning (Trivy), and optionally SBOM generation and image signing (Syft/CycloneDX + Cosign). DAST with OWASP ZAP runs against a deployed test environment. Gate on severity (fail on HIGH/CRITICAL), track suppressions in Git with a reason, and run heavy scans nightly to keep PR feedback fast.
Where should Flyway/Liquibase migrations run in CI/CD?

Run them once per deployment as a dedicated step or job (pipeline stage, Kubernetes Job, Helm pre-upgrade hook) before the new pods roll out, using a DB user with DDL rights that the app itself does not need. Running on application startup works for small apps (Flyway takes a lock), but with many replicas it slows startup and couples migration failures to pod crashes. Write migrations backward compatible so a rollback of the code does not require a rollback of the schema. In CI, validate migrations against a throwaway database (Testcontainers) on every PR.
How do you version build artifacts and Docker images?

Use SemVer for releases and attach the Git SHA (or build number) for traceability: orders:1.4.0-a1b2c3d. SNAPSHOT versions are for development only; release artifacts are immutable and published once. Release builds are usually triggered by a Git tag so code, artifact and image line up. Never deploy latest — you cannot tell what is running or roll back reliably; pin by tag or, better, by image digest.

disableConcurrentBuilds vs lock vs milestone?

| disableConcurrentBuilds() | lock('staging-env') | milestone()
Scope | One job (one branch in Multibranch) | Any job using the same resource name | Builds of the same job
Effect | Next build waits (or abortPrevious: true aborts the running one) | Only one build at a time inside the block | An older build cannot pass after a newer one has; it is aborted
Granularity | Whole build | A stage or block | A point in the pipeline
Needs a plugin | No | Lockable Resources | Pipeline: Milestone Step
Typical use | Jobs that are not safe to run twice | Shared test environment or database | Stop an old commit deploying over a newer one
Rule of thumb: lock the shared resource, not the whole job, so builds still run in parallel up to the risky part; add a milestone before deploy so the newest commit always wins.
sh vs sh(returnStatus: true) vs sh(returnStdout: true)?

| sh 'cmd' | returnStatus: true | returnStdout: true
Returns | Nothing | The exit code (int) | The output (String)
Non-zero exit code | Fails the step | Does not fail; you check the code | Fails the step
Output in the log | Yes | Yes | No, it is captured
Typical use | Build and test commands | "Does this file differ?" checks | Read a version or commit hash
def sha = sh(script: 'git rev-parse --short HEAD', returnStdout: true).trim()
def rc  = sh(script: 'git diff --quiet', returnStatus: true)
Interview tip: always .trim() captured output; the trailing newline breaks image tags and string comparisons.
